title: The reed flute
hookLine: the Masnavi opens with a reed cut from its reed-bed, crying to return (Masnavi 1, opening)

lines: A LONG POEM IN SIX BOOKS.
cards: Ever heard a sound that made you homesick for a place you couldn't name? A train horn at night. A song from a street you'll never walk again.
A flute in a movie that makes your chest ache for no reason. Rumi's great poem, the Masnavi, runs to six books. And the very first thing it asks isn't to believe or to study.
It's to listen. To one instrument: the ney, the reed flute of Persia and Turkey, breathy and low, a sound like someone sighing.

teach.b: In E. H. Whinfield's Victorian English translation, the Masnavi begins: "Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains."
It was cut from the reed bed where it grew, and ever since, it cries. Its cry, it says, has made men and women moan, because the song is a longing to go back. Think how a ney is made.
You cut a reed from the marsh, hollow it out, burn holes in it. It's empty inside.
And only because it's empty and cut off can breath pass through it and make music. The cry isn't a malfunction. It's the song.

Rumi's readers have understood the reed as the human soul. It came from God, was cut off and sent into the world, and its ache, a homesickness for a place it can't name, is the soul remembering where it came from.
The Qur'an has a line Muslims say when something is lost, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning."
Readers have heard the reed as that verse set to music. There's a second layer. A flute doesn't play itself; someone breathes through it.
Sufis read that as: the song is the player's, not the reed's. The reed's only job is to be hollow and let the breath through. That's why the Masnavi starts with listening.
Before any story or teaching, the poem asks for an ear.

how: Readers of the Masnavi often begin with its opening lines, the Song of the Reed, which are recited and sung in Persian; the ney is played in the Mevlevi ceremony and in Sufi gatherings across Turkey, Iran and beyond.

o: the Persian word for longing or homesickness
the reed flute that opens Rumi's Masnavi

games.q: the song of the reed — tap the pairs.

s: the Masnavi opens with a word to believe
it opens with a word to listen: hearken to the reed-flute.
the reed can sing only because it's hollow
cut and emptied, so breath can pass through it.
the Masnavi is a short poem

games.q: you're Rumi, beginning the long poem of your life. what's the very first thing you ask your reader to do?
games.why: the Masnavi begins with listening: hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains. the longing comes first.

practice: Breathe in slowly, all the way down, and on the out-breath hum one low, long note for as long as it lasts, feeling it in your chest and your face.
Let yourself be hollow, like the reed, and let the breath do the work, two or three times, then sit in the quiet after the sound. If you pray, you can let the note carry your longing to God.

wordCard.voice: Ney. The reed flute that opens Rumi's Masnavi, cut from its reed bed, crying to go home. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: the reed flute, the ney. the Masnavi is in Persian, and its first word is bishnaw, listen.

carryVoice: Your line: listen to the reed. Before the stories, before the teaching, the longing comes first. Until tomorrow.
